title: Kanishka's council
hook: the Kushan king's council in Kashmir, in the northern accounts

segments.voice: Yesterday: like the ocean, nibbana pointed to by simile. Your line: like space. Today we leave the king's court and head north.

Sheets of copper, engraved line after line with commentary on the teaching, sealed inside a stupa so the words would last. That is the story the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang recorded about Kashmir. A few days ago, the Theravada chronicles of Sri Lanka remembered a council under Ashoka, and a canon written on palm leaves. Travel north, into Kashmir and beyond, and the accounts kept there remember another gathering, under another king: Kanishka, a ruler of the Kushan empire.
screen: `COPPER SHEETS, SEALED IN A STUPA.` → `THE SOUTH REMEMBERS ITS COUNCILS.` → `THE NORTH REMEMBERS KANISHKA.`

segments.voice: First, the king. In the northern accounts, Kanishka is a powerful ruler who becomes a patron of the teaching. Tradition says he was troubled because the monks he consulted gave him different explanations of the same teachings, and he wanted to know which were sound. Second, the gathering. So, the accounts say, he called learned monks together in Kashmir. Some name a monk called Vasumitra as its leader, and some link the poet Ashvaghosha with it too. Others place the meeting somewhere else. The stories agree on the king and the purpose more than on the details. Third, the work. In these accounts the monks didn't write a new canon. They wrote commentaries: long explanations of the teaching and of the finer points of the Abhidharma, the systematic analysis of mind and experience. That's where the copper sheets come in: Xuanzang recorded a tradition that these commentaries were engraved on them and sealed inside a stupa. Fourth, why it matters that the accounts differ. The Theravada chronicles of Sri Lanka don't include this council in their list. The northern schools, and the Tibetan and Chinese histories that drew on them, remember it. Nobody has to decide here which list is right. Buddhism was already more than one living tradition, with more than one memory of its own past. Each community kept the councils that shaped its own texts. Hearing the northern account doesn't cancel the southern one. It's another community, telling the story the way it was told to them.
screen: `A KING TROUBLED BY MANY EXPLANATIONS.` · `LEARNED MONKS GATHER IN KASHMIR.` · `COMMENTARIES, SAID TO BE SEALED IN A STUPA.` · `NORTH AND SOUTH REMEMBER DIFFERENT COUNCILS.` · then, large: `THE NORTHERN ACCOUNT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something told or done one way where you grew up and another way somewhere else: a holiday, a recipe, a saint's story, the name for a meal. Let both versions sit side by side without choosing a winner, noticing what each place keeps and what it leaves out, then come back to the breath, which needs no version at all.
Kanishka's council. The gathering of monks in Kashmir under the Kushan king, remembered in the northern accounts, where commentaries on the teaching were composed.
Your line: the northern account. Another memory of the past, beside the southern one. Day eight hundred seventy-four, done.

chat.says: Why don't all Buddhists count Kanishka's council in their history?
options: The northern accounts remember it; Sri Lanka's chronicles simply don't list it.
It was proven a forgery, so every school has dropped it since then.
It came after the canon was closed, so it never counted for anyone.
chat.meaning: The Theravada chronicles don't include this council; the northern schools and the Tibetan and Chinese histories remember it. Each community kept its own memory.
